questions.stem: Which species acts as a Lewis acid in AlCl3 + Cl- -> AlCl4-?
options: None, since no proton is transferred
questions.explanation: AlCl3 has an empty orbital on aluminum and accepts an electron pair from Cl-. Chloride is the donor (Lewis base). AlCl4- is the product. The Lewis definition does not require protons, so the last option is wrong.
questions.subtopic: Acid and base definitions: Arrhenius, Bronsted-Lowry, Lewis

questions.stem: At pH 7.4, which phosphate species pair dominates (pKa2 = 7.20)?
questions.explanation: pH is 0.2 above pKa2, so the ratio is 10^0.2 = 1.6 HPO4 2- per H2PO4-. H3PO4 is minor above pH 4. PO4 3- appears only near pKa3 (12.35), and both species are present, not just H2PO4-.

questions.stem: A weak base B (0.10 M, pKb 4.75) is half-neutralized by HCl. The pH is:
questions.explanation: At half-equivalence [B] = [BH+], so pH = pKa of BH+ = 14 - 4.75 = 9.25. The value 4.75 is the pKb (a pOH here), 7.00 is for a strong acid and strong base, and 5.28 is the pH at full equivalence.

questions.stem: Ksp of PbI2 is 7.1 x 10^-9. Its molar solubility is closest to:
questions.explanation: Ksp = 4s^3, so s = (7.1e-9/4)^(1/3) = 1.2e-3 M. 8.4e-5 uses s^2 (the AB formula), 7.1e-9 is the Ksp itself, and 1.8e-3 uses the wrong power.

questions.stem: The osmotic pressure of 0.050 M CaCl2 at 300 K (R = 0.0821 L atm/mol K, i = 3) is closest to:
questions.explanation: pi = iMRT = 3 x 0.050 x 0.0821 x 300 = 3.7 atm. 1.2 atm omits i, 0.12 atm uses the wrong power of ten, and 11 atm is three times too large.

demo_cards.front: Arrhenius definition of an acid and a base?
demo_cards.back: An acid raises [H+] in water. A base raises [OH-] in water.

demo_cards.text: Bronsted-Lowry: an acid {{c1::donates}} a proton and a base {{c1::accepts}} a proton. Lewis: an acid {{c2::accepts}} an electron pair.

demo_cards.stem: Which species is the conjugate acid of HPO4 2-?
demo_cards.why: Add one proton to HPO4 2- to get H2PO4-. PO4 3- is its conjugate base. H3PO4 is two protons away.

demo_cards.statement: Every Bronsted-Lowry acid is also an Arrhenius acid.
demo_cards.why: Arrhenius acids must release H+ in water. Bronsted-Lowry also covers non-aqueous proton donors and acid-base reactions without water.
